title: Silver chloride in salty water
hook: A silver salt dissolves a little in pure water. Does salty water change how much?

knows: that salts dissolve only up to a limit
that dissolved salts are separate ions
doesNotKnow: that adding an ion already present lowers how much of the other ion can stay dissolved
that the two ions' concentrations multiply to a fixed ceiling

misconception: A salt's solubility is a fixed number of grams per litre, whatever else is in the water.
objective: The learner can say that in 0.10 mol/L chloride the silver ion concentration over AgCl crystals falls from about 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ to about 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol/L, because the product of the two ion concentrations has a fixed ceiling of about 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰.

claims.text: Silver chloride (AgCl) is a salt that dissolves only a little in water, giving silver ions (Ag⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻).
claims.source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, solubility product constants; AgCl is sparingly soluble.

claims.text: While AgCl crystals remain in the water, [Ag⁺] × [Cl⁻] equals about 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ (mol/L)² at 25 °C.
claims.source: Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C (CRC Handbook). Concentrations used in place of activities, an approximation.

claims.text: In pure water [Ag⁺] is about 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L.
In water with 0.10 mol/L of NaCl, [Ag⁺] is about 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol/L, about 7,500 times lower than in pure water (simple model that ignores AgCl₂⁻ complexes).
claims.source: [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ mol/L (the solved quadratic gives the same to 2 figures); 1.34 × 10⁻⁵ / 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ = 7,450 (node; Demo.tsx RATIO). Ignores activity and soluble AgCl₂⁻ complexes, which matter more at higher chloride. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 13): node: sqrt(1.8e-10) = 1.342e-5; quadratic free [Ag+] at 0.10 M Cl- = 1.80e-9; ratio 7,454, Demo.tsx RATIO rounds to 7,500. Model limitation stated in text.

claims.text: The intermediate steps, 0.001 and 0.010 mol/L of NaCl, give [Ag⁺] of about 1.8 × 10⁻⁷ and 1.8 × 10⁻⁸ mol/L.
claims.source: 1.8e-10 / 0.001 = 1.8e-7; 1.8e-10 / 0.01 = 1.8e-8 (node; the exact quadratic differs by under 0.1%).

claims.text: Adding one of the ions already in the solution lowers how much of the other can stay dissolved (the common-ion effect).
claims.source: Atkins, Physical Chemistry / Chemical Principles, common-ion effect; Chemistry LibreTexts.

claims.text: Square brackets mean moles per litre: [Ag⁺] is the number of moles of silver ions in each litre.

While crystals remain, the two ion concentrations multiplied have a ceiling (1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰); piling in chloride makes silver drop out as crystals to keep the product at the ceiling, so solubility is not one fixed number: it shifts when the water already holds one of the ions.
claims.source: CONCERN from the fact-checker: the 7,500-fold drop is for free [Ag+] only. Using stability constants log beta1 = 3.04 (AgCl aq) and log beta2 = 5.04 (AgCl2-), total dissolved silver is about 1.4e-5 mol/L in pure water and only about 2.2e-6 mol/L at 0.10 mol/L NaCl, a drop of roughly 6 times, and it rises again near 1 mol/L (about 2e-5). The word 'solubility' in the reveal therefore overstates what the model shows. Suggest 'the free silver ion concentration shifts', or state that AgCl2- is ignored (the Demo.tsx header and c4 source already say so). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-13; needs an independent check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Independent check of the pass-8 concern. node: free [Ag+] = Ksp/[Cl-] is 1.8e-9 at 0.10 mol/L (c4 holds even with complexes). With log beta1 3.04, log beta2 5.04, total dissolved silver is 1.35e-5 (pure) vs 2.1e-6 mol/L (0.10 mol/L), so real AgCl solubility still falls about 6x and silver does precipitate; 'solubility shifts' is literally true (it falls, then rises above about 0.5 mol/L). The 7,500x figure in the reveal is attached to [Ag+], not to solubility. Verified as written. Non-blocking suggestion for the builder: add 'ignores AgCl2- complexes' to the stage note. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 13): Pass 13 independent re-check: with log b1 3.04, log b2 5.04, total dissolved Ag is 1.36e-5 (pure) vs 2.17e-6 M (0.10 M NaCl), so solubility does shift; the product ceiling statement is the Ksp definition. Verified as written.

claims.text: At 0.10 mol/L of NaCl, about 99.99% of the silver that dissolves in pure water returns to the crystals (1 − 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ ÷ 1.3 × 10⁻⁵).

recall.question: A sparingly soluble salt has an ion-product ceiling of 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ (mol/L)². If the water already holds 0.01 mol/L of the salt's negative ion, the positive ion's concentration over crystals is about…
recall.why: The ceiling divided by the existing ion's concentration: 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 0.01 = 1 × 10⁻⁸ mol/L.
